claims.text: A refractory ceramic or intermetallic matrix can serve as the high-strength host for the proposed self-lubricating composite.
Spark plasma sintering can produce an in-situ layered lubricant phase within the refractory matrix.
Spark plasma sintering can precisely control the spatial distribution and size of an embedded MoS2 phase.
The intervention will create a uniformly distributed, finely controlled microstructure of layered lubricant phases.
Embedded MoS2 provides lubrication by facilitating shear between its layers.
The refractory host matrix resists deformation and retains mechanical strength under extreme operating conditions.
In-situ formation and precise dispersion of MoS2 mitigate the detrimental effects associated with randomly added lubricant phases.
The engineered composite will maintain low friction across a wide temperature range.
The engineered composite will maintain low wear across a wide temperature range.
The engineered composite will preserve high mechanical strength across a wide temperature range.
The engineered composite will outperform composites having uncontrolled lubricant dispersion in friction, wear, and retained mechanical strength.
Random dispersion of conventionally added MoS2 often compromises composite mechanical strength at elevated temperatures.
Performance depends on optimizing the volume fraction and dispersion parameters of the lubricant phase.
Adequate interfacial bonding between the lubricant phase and matrix is necessary for the proposed performance.
